claims.text: Service-relevant thermal and mechanical loading activates diffusion-driven grain-boundary modifications in initially homogeneous, single-phase high-entropy alloys.
The grain-boundary modifications consist of localized chemical ordering or segregation.
Localized chemical ordering or segregation reduces grain-boundary cohesion.
Reduced grain-boundary cohesion facilitates intergranular crack initiation.
Intergranular crack initiation caused by grain-boundary chemical modification decreases toughness.
The proposed mechanism is distinct from conventional precipitation and segregation mechanisms in traditional alloys.
The initial alloy has a homogeneous, single-phase, compositionally complex matrix with clean grain boundaries.
Combined thermal cycling and cyclic or slow tensile loading can promote grain-boundary chemical ordering or segregation.
Diffusion can be activated under service-relevant temperatures and loading rates while the overall single-phase structure is preserved.
Grain-boundary chemical heterogeneities produce local regions of increased stiffness.
Grain-boundary chemical heterogeneities produce local regions of reduced ductility.
Applied thermal and mechanical stresses enhance atomic diffusion at grain boundaries.
Treated samples with enhanced grain-boundary ordering or segregation will have lower fracture toughness than the baseline.
Treated samples with enhanced grain-boundary ordering or segregation will exhibit a shift toward intergranular crack propagation.
The as-processed baseline has minimal grain-boundary chemical heterogeneity.
The as-processed baseline has high fracture toughness.
The mechanism may not manifest under static, low-temperature, or high-strain-rate conditions because diffusion kinetics are altered.
The diffusion kinetics and degree of local ordering required for measurable embrittlement have not been quantitatively determined.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis calls the proposed mechanism distinct from conventional precipitation/segregation mechanisms, yet segregation is itself one of the two central proposed mediators. No distinction in segregating species, thermodynamics, morphology, or causal action is supplied.
